newsitem.title: JORDAN: Prominent Jordanians join election boycott call.
newsitem.headline: Prominent Jordanians join election boycott call.

text.p: Prominent Jordanian public figures on Monday joined ranks with those supporting an election boycott call by Islamists to protest government policies.

Eighty independent public figures representing a broad spectrum of opinion endorsed July's move by the Moslem Brotherhood movement, which commands widespread grass-roots support, to boycott the November national elections.
Among the signatories to a publicly released statement are two former prime ministers, Ahmad Obeidat and Taher al Masri, along with scores of lawyers, former deputies and businessmen.
"There has been a coup against the democratic experiment," the statement said.
It accused the government of "adopting policies which put curbs on public freedoms and limited political and party activity and applied repression in dealing with civic institutions."

The Brotherhood's boycott move has galvanised the local political scene. It forced its political arm, the Islamic Action Front, the largest political party which held 16 of the 80 parliamentary seats, to make a similar move.

Most of the smaller secular leftist and pan-Arab parties also heeded the call despite tactical divisions on how to deal with Prime Minister Abdul-Salam al-Majali's government on terms for ending the boycott.

Those signing the statement criticised successive governments for what they described as policies that have brought the country to the brink of calamity by fuelling a "dangerous political and economic crisis".
They said those policies were dealing a serious blow to the country's nascent democratic experiment.
It was launched in 1989 by King Hussein after a severe crisis that sparked countrywide riots.
The November elections would be the first since Jordan's 1994 peace treaty with Israel, which the Islamic and secular opposition regard as a capitulation and want to see revoked.
The government has brushed aside Islamists' demands to revoke interim laws on the press and the economy that were issued during a parliamentary recess.
Under pressure to find a way out of the boycott crisis as the election date approaches, however, the government is now sending conciliatory signals.
It says it is willing to engage the Islamists in an dialogue to resolve current differences.
But opposition sources say Majali's government is dragging its feet on setting a date to start a serious debate on their grievances.
